paragraphs.heading: Jupiter's innermost big moon
paragraphs.text: Io is the innermost of Jupiter's four Galilean moons and the second smallest of them. It is a little larger than Earth's Moon. Among all the natural satellites in the Solar System, it ranks fourth by size. Of all moons it has the highest density and the strongest surface gravity. By atomic ratio, it also holds less water than any other known object in the Solar System.

paragraphs.heading: Heated from within
paragraphs.text: With more than 400 active volcanoes, Io is the most geologically active body in the Solar System. The heat comes from friction deep inside Io as Jupiter, Europa and Ganymede all pull on it, a process called tidal heating. Most moons in the outer Solar System are largely water ice, but Io is mostly silicate rock around a core of molten iron or iron sulfide.

paragraphs.heading: Plumes, lava and mountains
paragraphs.text: Some volcanoes throw plumes of sulfur and sulfur dioxide up to 500 km above the ground. Many lava flows streak the surface, a few of them more than 500 km long. Over 100 mountains rise from it, pushed up by heavy compression at the base of the silicate crust, and some stand taller than Mount Everest. Most of the rest is broad plains frosted with sulfur and sulfur dioxide.

paragraphs.heading: A colourful, changing face
paragraphs.text: Io's volcanoes explain many of its unusual features. Plumes and lava flows change the surface a great deal and tint it yellow, red, white, black and green, largely through different forms and compounds of sulfur. When the two Voyager spacecraft passed in 1979, they found a young surface with no obvious impact craters.

paragraphs.heading: Reaching out to Jupiter
paragraphs.text: The material from the volcanoes makes up Io's thin, patchy atmosphere. It also strongly shapes Jupiter's huge magnetosphere and its radiation levels. Matter thrown out by Io forms a large, intense plasma torus around Jupiter, which makes the space on and around the moon harsh with radiation. Visiting spacecraft found a belt of high-energy radiation running along the path of Io's orbit.

paragraphs.heading: Discovery and naming
paragraphs.text: Galileo Galilei first saw Io on 7 January 1610 with a 20x telescope at the University of Padua, but it blurred together with Europa into one point of light. The next night he saw them apart, and the IAU uses 8 January 1610 as Io's discovery date. He published the find in Sidereus Nuncius in March 1610. Simon Marius later claimed he found the moons in 1609, a week before Galileo, and his names, including Io, were not widely used until the mid-20th century. Before then Io was usually called Jupiter I.

paragraphs.heading: Why Io mattered
paragraphs.text: The Galilean moons helped astronomy adopt the Copernican model of the Solar System and develop Kepler's laws of planetary motion. The first measurement of the speed of light relied on Io in particular. The Galileo spacecraft made several close flybys in the 1990s and early 2000s, learning about its interior and what its surface is made of. Cassini–Huygens, New Horizons and Juno have watched it since, along with Hubble and telescopes on Earth.
